notes: Seed set. Coordinates are approximate, taken from street intersections, and must be checked against Sanborn maps. Teasers are written in our own words; the full story lives at each source link. Photo image URLs follow the OpenSFHistory pattern and have not been fetched from the build machine, so check they load. Status is draft or published; only published stories show in the app.

stories.title: The ballpark beside the park
stories.teaser: A semi pro ballpark filled this block next to Golden Gate Park, with cable cars running to the gate and a saloon tucked under the grandstands. About 10,000 people came for opening day in 1887. The first Stanford and California Big Games were played here before the land was sold for houses.

photos.caption: A game between the Haverlys and the Pioneers at the Haight Street Grounds
photos.credit: J. A. Todd, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp33.00518

photos.caption: Cable cars at Haight and Stanyan, by the old ballpark entrance
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp13.234

stories.verification_notes: Location per the 1889 Sanborn map as described by SF Story: Stanyan between Frederick and Waller; Wikipedia says bounded by Stanyan, Waller, Shrader and Frederick. The Big Game claim comes from Wikipedia only.

stories.title: Shoot the Chutes on Haight Street
stories.teaser: A block from the park stood the Chutes, an amusement ground whose star ride sent riders down a steep slide into an artificial lake. It added a roller coaster, a zoo and a vaudeville theater, then moved to Fulton Street in 1902 and later to Fillmore and Playland.

source.title: Architecture Spotlight: Chutes in the Haight
source.author: Untapped Cities

photos.caption: The waterslide at the Haight Chutes on opening day
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.1133

stories.verification_notes: Between Clayton and Cole on Haight per Untapped Cities. Add a second source and an OpenSFHistory photo. OpenSFHistory describes the site as bounded by Haight, Waller, Cole and Clayton, and places it at 37.7692, -122.4504. A second text source is still wanted.

stories.title: From movie house to rock dances
stories.teaser: A neighborhood movie theater opened on this corner in 1910 and later grew to about 1,500 seats. After it stopped showing films in 1964 it became the Straight Theater, a home for 1960s rock dances. The building was torn down in the late 1970s and a Goodwill stands here now.

photos.caption: The closed Haight Theatre at Haight and Cole before its summer 1979 demolition
photos.credit: Greg Gaar, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp67.0095

photos.caption: Haight Theatre ad for August 2, 1914
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp67.0039

stories.verification_notes: 1702 Haight at Cole. Demolition is given as August 1979 in the main article and 1981 in comments; confirm. Dates and events of the Straight Theater period (1966 to 1967) need a second source such as the Straight Theater history site. The OpenSFHistory caption for the May 1979 photo says the theatre was demolished in summer 1979, which supports the 1979 date over 1981.

stories.title: The Psychedelic Shop
stories.teaser: Brothers Jay and Ron Thelin opened a head shop at 1535 Haight Street in January 1966, selling incense, posters, records and clothing. It became a gathering place for the counterculture. They closed it for good on October 6, 1967, the day of the Death of Hippie ceremony, and gave away what was left.

source.title: This Day in Cannabis History: the Psychedelic Shop
source.author: World of Cannabis Museum

stories.verification_notes: Address from the museum page; the exact spot on the block needs checking. The Death of Hippie date (Oct 6, 1967, Buena Vista Park) comes from Wikipedia's Haight-Ashbury article. Find a stronger historical source.

stories.title: The comedy club at Carl and Cole
stories.teaser: In the 1980s The Other Cafe at 100 Carl Street became a full time comedy club and an early stage for comics including Robin Williams, Dana Carvey and Whoopi Goldberg. The corner now holds a crepe restaurant.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Confirm the performers and that the tenant is still Crepes on Cole. Look for a Western Neighborhoods Project or newspaper source.

stories.title: The college that became a hospital
stories.teaser: Doctors and students from the Affiliated Colleges on this slope helped run relief care after the 1906 earthquake, while the Army ran a field hospital in Golden Gate Park. The disaster pushed a planned teaching hospital to the top of the list, and the first UC Hospital opened here in April 1907.

source.title: 1906 earthquake spurs rapid response at Parnassus
source.author: UCSF

stories.verification_notes: UCSF Library's history site (history.library.ucsf.edu) has period photos with open reuse notes; add one.

stories.title: The world's fair in the park
stories.teaser: In 1894 a fair of about 200 acres filled the park around today's Music Concourse, with roughly 120 buildings and more than two million visitors. Most of it was taken down afterward, but the Japanese Tea Garden and the Concourse were kept.

source.title: 125 years ago: Midwinter International Exposition in Golden Gate Park
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Crowd at the first shovelful of sand for the Midwinter Fair site
photos.credit: Isaiah West Taber, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.01330

photos.caption: The Bonet Electric Tower at the Midwinter Fair
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.075

stories.verification_notes: Opening day photo is by Isaiah West Taber via the Western Neighborhoods Project; find its OpenSFHistory id.

stories.title: The streetcar graveyard
stories.teaser: This whole block between Irving, Lincoln Way, 14th and Funston was once a yard where retired streetcars waited for the scrapper among the Sunset sand. It was planned as a carhouse in 1907 and later served Muni as a storage lot.

photos.caption: Aerial view of the streetcar boneyard, looking west on Irving at 14th Avenue
photos.credit: Via SFMTA blog; original source to confirm

stories.verification_notes: The SFMTA post points to a Western Neighborhoods Project article and podcast episode 182; make that the primary source.

stories.title: Many lives of a corner
stories.teaser: In the early 1970s the southeast corner of Ninth and Irving held a bar called The Stein, also known as Mac's Place, with green streetcars rattling past. A Jamba Juice came later, and a French chicken sandwich restaurant was announced for the space in 2025.

source.title: Then and Now: Ninth Avenue and Irving Street
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Ninth Avenue and Irving Street with a dentist above a pharmacy
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.11201

photos.caption: Mac's Place, The Stein, on the southeast corner of Ninth Avenue and Irving Street (postcard)
photos.credit: Private collector / Western Neighborhoods Project / OpenSFHistory

stories.verification_notes: Check whether the French restaurant opened as announced before showing the last sentence.

stories.title: The bakery's earlier self
stories.teaser: In November 1904 this Ninth Avenue building, between Irving and Judah, looked very different from the busy bakery it holds today at 1331 Ninth Avenue. A photo from the neighborhood archive shows it in its early days.

source.title: Historical Photo: Popular Inner Sunset shop long before customer lines
source.author: Richmond Review and Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: 9th Avenue near Irving, the site of today's Arizmendi Bakery
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4162

photos.caption: The Ninth Avenue building between Irving and Judah, November 1904
photos.credit: Private collector / Western Neighborhoods Project / OpenSFHistory

stories.verification_notes: Light entry. Find the story of the building's first occupant before publishing.

stories.title: The orphanage on the dunes
stories.teaser: In 1905 a purpose built brick home for children opened here, out among the sand dunes. Seven months later the 1906 earthquake wrecked it, yet every one of the 59 children inside got out unhurt. They camped on the dunes for twelve days.

photos.caption: The Nursery for Homeless Children on the north side of Lake Street between 14th and 15th Avenues
photos.credit: San Francisco Public Library, AAD-5883

stories.verification_notes: A 1906 newspaper transcription places the Nursery at 13th and Lake; annual reports and SF Story say 14th. Confirm on the Sanborn map.

stories.title: The orphanage that fell apart
stories.teaser: A few blocks east stood the Maria Kip Orphanage, which a 1906 report called the most complete ruin among the city's children's homes. All 125 children inside at the moment of the quake survived.

source.title: Every institution in the city for care of children damaged
source.author: 1906 newspaper account, transcribed
source.publisher: Museum of the City of San Francisco

photos.caption: The Maria Kip Orphanage, Lake Street near 7th Avenue, damaged after the 1906 earthquake
photos.credit: Harry O. Wood, Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley, BANC PIC 1957.007 Ser.1:115

stories.verification_notes: Confirm the 125 figure and the building's later fate in a second source.

stories.title: The farm at the edge of the Presidio
stories.teaser: Before the avenues filled in, a small farm ran along the Presidio boundary here. The Bauchou family lived at 9 14th Avenue, and in 1905 they were the new orphanage's nearest neighbors, with Mountain Lake visible down the slope.

photos.caption: Bauchou home on 14th Avenue, view east toward Mountain Lake
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.207

stories.verification_notes: OpenSFHistory caption names Bernard Bauchou as the occupant of 9 14th Avenue.

stories.title: The refugee shack that started a movement
stories.teaser: Behind a plain Sunset facade stand three 1906 relief cottages joined together, with a fourth in the backyard. Jane Cryan moved in during 1982, learned what they were and fought for them. In 1984 the city landmarked the house, the only refugee shack it has ever protected.

source.title: This tiny SF shack tipped off a decades long preservation movement
source.author: Keith Menconi

stories.verification_notes: Address 1227 24th Avenue and Landmark No. 171 per the Examiner; Atlas Obscura confirms Cryan's 1982 lease and Landmark 171. The 1984 landmark year comes from the Examiner only. Pin placed on the block, not the lot.

stories.title: Iceland on 48th Avenue
stories.teaser: Inside an ordinary Outer Sunset block, a barn like building held a full size ice rink from 1926. Kids learned to skate and played junior hockey while the surf rolled a few streets away. Insurance costs and decay ended it, and the rink came down in 1991 for condominiums.

photos.caption: Interior of the San Francisco Ice Arena
photos.credit: Greg Gaar, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp72.16436

stories.verification_notes: Address 1557 48th Avenue per SF Story; opened March 1926, demolished July 8, 1991. Pin placed on the block.

stories.title: The castle on Strawberry Hill
stories.teaser: A reddish concrete lookout with little bastion towers once crowned Strawberry Hill, the park's highest point, paid for by Thomas Sweeny. Carriages rolled up for the panorama and a waterfall tumbled toward Stow Lake. The 1906 earthquake wrecked it, and parts of the foundation remain today.

photos.caption: Sweeny's Observatory on Strawberry Hill
photos.credit: Isaiah West Taber, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.397

photos.caption: The observatory in ruins after the earthquake
photos.credit: James Stoddard, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.5474

stories.verification_notes: Dedicated Sept 19, 1891 and ruined April 18, 1906 per SF Story. Pin set on Strawberry Hill summit; remains are near it.

stories.title: The janitor who ran the saloon
stories.teaser: In 1895 a roadhouse nicknamed the Milk Punch House stood beside the Laguna Honda School on Seventh Avenue. Its owner, Irish born Elizabeth Chadwick, also worked as the school janitor while raising three children upstairs. A grand jury objected, the school board argued for months and parents signed petitions in her defense.

photos.caption: The Laguna Honda School, damaged in 1906, with the saloon beside it
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.1265

stories.verification_notes: School stood on 7th Avenue between Irving and Judah, saloon just north of it, per SF Story. The article does not say whether the saloon building survives.

stories.title: A house on the dunes, still standing
stories.teaser: House painter Elbert Dodge bought four lots on bare dunes in 1903 and spent a year of Sundays and holidays building a home with his brother. He added strawberries, fruit trees, chickens and a windmill well. The Chronicle admired him in 1905, and the house still stands on 22nd Avenue.
stories.verification_notes: Address 1549 22nd Avenue per SF Story. Pin placed on the block. Private home, view from the street.

stories.title: The day a twister took a Sunset house
stories.teaser: On February 24, 1930, a storm shoved a lone house at 46th Avenue and Ortega off its foundation and left it leaning in the sand. Police first heard reports of an explosion. Owner John Volz was at work, lost about 5,000 dollars and rebuilt with a ground floor garage.

photos.caption: The house knocked off its foundation after the storm
photos.credit: Emiliano Echeverria, Randolph Brandt Collection, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp30.0124

stories.verification_notes: Address 1896 46th Avenue per SF Story, which also corrects newspaper claims that the house spun 90 degrees.

stories.title: A flight school on the sand
stories.teaser: In 1914 the Christofferson brothers taught flying on the sand at the foot of Sloat Boulevard, just as the Great Highway was being built. Their daredevil circle was short lived. Several of the pilots tied to the school, including Silas Christofferson in 1916, were killed in crashes within a few years.
stories.verification_notes: Location described as at the foot of Sloat Boulevard near the Great Highway; the exact hangar site is not given, so the pin is approximate. No archive photo IDs listed in the article.

stories.title: The hog ranch at 14th and Lincoln
stories.teaser: Cornelius Reynolds, an English immigrant, claimed dunes near today's 14th Avenue and Lincoln Way in the 1860s and raised hogs, then ran a small saloon. Family deaths came one after another. After 1906 he sold land to the streetcar company. Apartments now cover the ranch, though its old boundary still shows.

photos.caption: View from Strawberry Hill over the western dunes
photos.credit: Charles Turrill, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4937

photos.caption: The Inner Sunset seen from Mount Sutro
photos.credit: W. C. Billington, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.569

stories.verification_notes: Ranch location per SF Story: 14th Avenue and Lincoln Way (then H Street). Sits near our streetcar boneyard card; the two stories overlap on the same block.

stories.title: Making 19th Avenue
stories.teaser: Around 1900 19th Avenue was mostly a line on a map, with Carl Larsen's chicken ranch near today's Noriega and Ortega. A rutted track was paved by 1916, and a 1929 right of way near Lake Merced let it connect south. After the Golden Gate Bridge, it was widened into Highway 1.

photos.caption: View north from Moraga Street over the dunes
photos.credit: Charles Turrill, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.713

photos.caption: Fresh paving near Quintara Street
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, Department of Public Works, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp36.01322

stories.verification_notes: Larsen ranch between Noriega and Ortega per SF Story; the pin is placed there.

stories.title: The Mothers Building
stories.teaser: Herbert and Mortimer Fleishhacker gave this Italian Renaissance rest house in 1925 in memory of their mother, a refuge for mothers and children beside the zoo. Women artists added Noah's Ark murals in the 1930s. It closed in 2002 as unsafe and still waits for repairs.

photos.caption: The new Mothers Building and wading pool
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.1412

photos.caption: Children at the wading pool
photos.credit: Gabriel Moulin, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.4762

stories.verification_notes: Architect George Kelham; city landmark 2022. Inside the zoo grounds, so the building is only visible from zoo property.

stories.title: The last roadhouse
stories.teaser: Hidden behind redwoods below 19th Avenue, the Trocadero opened in 1892 as a roadhouse known for turtle soup. Political boss Abe Ruef was arrested here in 1907. It later served as a women's outdoor club. A falling eucalyptus smashed the roof in 2023, and restoration finished in 2025.

photos.caption: Postcard advertisement for the Trocadero
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.03678

photos.caption: View past the turtle pond
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.1604

stories.verification_notes: City landmark 301 (April 5, 2022) per SF Story. Pin placed on the slope in Stern Grove below 19th Avenue.

stories.title: Parkside on the dunes
stories.teaser: The first Parkside homes rose on dunes near Vicente and 32nd Avenue in 1907, sold by the Parkside Realty Company. Residents formed an improvement club in 1908 to demand services, and Eugene Williams opened the district's first grocery in 1909. The L Taraval streetcar arrived in 1923.
stories.verification_notes: Commercial hub at Taraval and 32nd Avenue per SF Story; the first homes were slightly south, so the pin is approximate. The article also covers discriminatory covenants of the era.

stories.title: A steam engine on the zoo playground
stories.teaser: In August 1957 Southern Pacific donated switch engine 1294 to the zoo playground. A crane company moved it for free, local Teamsters paid for climbing bars, and children rang its bell for decades. Fog corroded the engine, and it was removed and scrapped around 1981.

photos.caption: The engine surprises the crowd on moving day
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.2963

photos.caption: The engine backs into the playground
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.2964

stories.verification_notes: Dedicated Nov 29, 1957. The article gives both early 1980s removal and 1981 scrapping, so the end date is stated loosely.

stories.title: The biggest pool in America
stories.teaser: Opened in 1925 beside the Great Highway, Fleishhacker Pool was billed as the largest swimming pool in the United States, 1,000 feet long and filled with seawater. Lifeguards patrolled in rowboats. Storm damage to a pipe in 1971 doomed it, and it was filled in and turned into zoo parking.

photos.caption: View south toward the Fleishhacker Pool site from the foot of Sloat Boulevard
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, SF Department of Public Works, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp36.02798

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia, read Oct 21, 2026). Pool house burned December 1, 2012. Pin on the former pool site, now parking; exact outline not checked.

stories.title: Opening day for the Sunset Tunnel
stories.teaser: On October 21, 1928, thousands came to the western portal at Carl and Cole to watch Mayor Sunny Jim Rolph pilot a streetcar through the new tunnel. The line to the ocean made the Sunset practical to live in. Digging had begun in 1926 and cost about 1.5 million dollars.

photos.caption: Mayor James Rolph at the controls of the first N line streetcar through the tunnel, near Carl and Cole
photos.credit: Horace Chaffee, SF Department of Public Works, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.0493

photos.caption: Tunnel construction on Carl near Cole
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.496

stories.verification_notes: Opening day facts from SFMTA; groundbreaking June 10, 1926 and cost $1,477,618 from Wikipedia's Sunset Tunnel page. Pin moved to OpenSFHistory's map point for the dedication photo.

stories.title: Kezar Stadium
stories.teaser: Willis Polk's stadium opened in Golden Gate Park in 1925 and later became the first home of the 49ers, who played here until 1970. Nearly 60,000 seats held the crowds. It hosted concerts afterward, and the original stadium was torn down in 1989 for a smaller rebuild.

source.title: Kezar Stadium: San Francisco's Pro Football Roots
source.author: Jeremy Menzies

photos.caption: A man works on seating during construction of Kezar Stadium
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.0039

photos.caption: Crowds fill the stands for the 1950 Shrine East West Game
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp25.5346

stories.verification_notes: Dates cross checked with Wikipedia (dedication May 2, 1925; demolition and rebuild 1989). Architect credit is SFMTA's. Pin moved to the OpenSFHistory map point for Kezar photos.

stories.title: From almshouse to hospital
stories.teaser: Laguna Honda began in 1867 as an almshouse for the poor and sick, on 87 acres where residents grew food and kept dairy cows. After the 1906 earthquake a 1,000 bed wing opened and was dedicated in 1909 by Theodore Roosevelt. The Spanish Revival main buildings followed in 1926.

photos.caption: The almshouse on the future site of Laguna Honda Hospital
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp15.777

photos.caption: Laguna Honda Hospital with Mount Sutro and Twin Peaks behind
photos.credit: Turrill & Miller, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.7885

stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Coordinates from the article's infobox.

stories.title: The arboretum that waited fifty years
stories.teaser: John McLaren sketched plans for an arboretum in the 1880s, but money never came. Then Helene Strybing left a bequest in 1927. WPA workers began planting in 1937 and the arboretum opened in May 1940. Today it is the San Francisco Botanical Garden, entered at Ninth Avenue and Lincoln.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Pin on the Ninth Avenue gate area.

stories.title: The tower people loved to hate
stories.teaser: When Sutro Tower went up in 1973, many neighbors hated it. Columnist Herb Caen joked it would stalk down the hill and attack the Golden Gate Bridge. Lights on its legs were removed after public outcry. It gathered TV transmitters that had been scattered across Bay Area hilltops.
stories.verification_notes: Single source (Wikipedia). Completed July 4, 1973. Tower sits on Clarendon Heights just above Cole Valley and the Inner Sunset.

stories.title: The streetcar that ate the dunes
stories.teaser: In 1910 the United Railroads built a special streetcar that scooped sand from the dunes around 21st Avenue and Ortega Street and loaded it onto work cars. Sand gives steel wheels grip on rails. Muni still sands its vehicles, but the dunes were long ago built over.
stories.verification_notes: Location and 1910 date from the SFMTA caption. Photos are in the SFMTA archive; no OpenSFHistory ID given.

stories.title: The L Taraval begins
stories.teaser: On April 12, 1919, small streetcars began shuttling from West Portal to Taraval and 33rd Avenue, Muni's thirteenth line. Riders transferred to the K to reach downtown. Tracks reached 48th Avenue in 1923, and a WPA extension in 1937 brought the line to 46th and Wawona, serving the zoo and pool.

source.title: Dunes to Destinations: 100 Years on the L Taraval
source.author: Jeremy Menzies

photos.caption: L line Magic Carpet car 1005 on Taraval near 23rd Avenue
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.50416

photos.caption: An L line car passes the Richfield station at Taraval and 28th Avenue
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp14.1507

stories.verification_notes: Dates from the SFMTA article. Pin at the original Taraval and 33rd terminal.

stories.title: The velodrome at Baker and Fell
stories.teaser: A banana shaped bicycle track and grandstand opened at Baker and Fell on November 21, 1896. Too few paying fans came, so promoters tried rugby, push ball and fireworks. The last races ran on October 3, 1897, and the track went to East Oakland. Later Southern Pacific built a hospital here.

photos.caption: View from Buena Vista Park north to the Panhandle and the velodrome
photos.credit: D. H. Wulzen, courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp13.032

photos.caption: The Southern Pacific Hospital at Fell and Baker
photos.credit: OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp37.02742

stories.verification_notes: Northwest corner of Baker and Fell per SF Story. The article does not say what is on the block today.

stories.title: Ground zero at Haight and Ashbury
stories.teaser: This Colonial Revival corner building at Haight and Ashbury was raised in 1907 to add storefronts. In the 1960s it housed an early hippie boutique, Mnasidika, at 1510 Haight, and is tied to Janis Joplin and the Grateful Dead. The city made it a landmark in 2006.

source.title: San Francisco Historic Landmark: Doolan-Larson Residence and Storefronts
source.author: NoeHill

stories.verification_notes: Landmark 253 approved July 14, 2006 per NoeHill; Wikipedia's Haight-Ashbury article adds the National Register listing. The Joplin and Dead links are loose and not detailed in the source.

stories.title: The funeral of the hippie
stories.teaser: On October 6, 1967, the Diggers carried a coffin down Haight Street to mark the death of the hippie. Mourners burned underground papers and clothes and knelt at Haight and Ashbury. The aim was to end media hype and the selling of the movement after the Summer of Love.

source.title: Death of Hippie: An end to the Summer of Love
source.author: UC Santa Cruz Library

stories.verification_notes: Funeral notice named Buena Vista Park; the procession ran down Haight Street per the exhibit. Wikipedia places the staged funeral at Buena Vista Park. Pin set at the kneel in corner.

stories.title: The first free clinic
stories.teaser: As tens of thousands of young people poured into the Haight in the Summer of Love, Dr. David Smith opened a free clinic on June 7, 1967. It became the model for hundreds more across the country. Bill Graham's benefit concerts helped keep it open until it closed in 2019.
stories.verification_notes: Opening date confirmed by Wikipedia and 730stanyan.org. Street address was NOT confirmed in a fetched source, so the pin is only the general area of Haight and Clayton. Check before sharing.

stories.title: The city's oldest library building
stories.teaser: Opened on October 29, 1909 at 1833 Page Street, the Park Branch was the first San Francisco branch built with public money. The McDougall Brothers designed it. A mural went up in 1975 and a renovation finished in 2011, though the 1989 earthquake cost it its circular skylights.
stories.verification_notes: Address per SF Story; pin is approximate along Page Street. Photos exist at SFPL (AAC-5839, AAC-5848) but no stable page URL was checked.

stories.title: A library on an empty block
stories.teaser: When the Sunset Branch Library opened on March 25, 1918, it stood alone on its block at Irving and 19th Avenue, built for under 44,000 dollars. The site had been an old barn that neighbors disliked because boys used it for target practice. Jefferson Elementary now fills the lot beside it.

source.title: Then and Now: Irving Street at 19th Avenue
source.author: Sunset Beacon

photos.caption: Irving Street at 19th Avenue, a few years before the library opened
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp26.1833

photos.caption: Children in soldier costumes on the library grounds at 19th and Irving
photos.credit: Courtesy of a private collector, OpenSFHistory / Western Neighborhoods Project, wnp27.1994

stories.verification_notes: Opening date and cost per the Sunset Beacon caption of a 1920 photo.

stories.title: A streetcar meets a tar truck
stories.teaser: Around 1940 a streetcar collided with a roofing tar truck at Fourth Avenue and Irving Street, a sticky scene someone photographed. The Sunset Beacon matched it with a modern view from the same spot, where trees and a UCSF building now stand and the parking has changed.

source.title: Then and Now: Fourth Avenue and Irving Street
source.author: Sunset Beacon

stories.verification_notes: Thin: a single photo caption. Included as a light event card.

stories.title: 710 Ashbury
stories.teaser: Members of the Grateful Dead shared this house at 710 Ashbury Street in the mid 1960s. In 1967 police arrested band members here for drug possession. The band answered with a press conference on the premises, arguing marijuana should be decriminalized and that local police were singling them out.
stories.verification_notes: HELD AS DRAFT: single tertiary source (Clio, citing Lonely Planet). Its own dates conflict (1965 to 1968 versus 1967). Needs a second source.

stories.title: The Red House on Haight
stories.teaser: Jimi Hendrix is believed to have lived for a time in an apartment above a shop at 1524A Haight Street, a few doors from the main intersection. The building is painted red in his honor, which gives it the name Red House. It is a private residence, so look from the street.
stories.verification_notes: HELD AS DRAFT: the source says details of his stay are sparse and uses hedged language. Needs a second source.
